blocks.body:
Differentiation is a mechanical process: the rules for sums, products, quotients and compositions turn any formula into its derivative. Integration goes the other way, and there is no such mechanical procedure. Given $x \cos x$, or $\dfrac{1}{x^2 - 1}$, or $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$, you have to find a function whose derivative it is, and the rules have to be run backwards.

This lesson collects the standard ways of doing that. Each one is a differentiation rule read in reverse: substitution undoes the chain rule, integration by parts undoes the product rule, and partial fractions is algebra that breaks a fraction into pieces whose antiderivatives are already known. By the [[ftc|fundamental theorem of calculus]], finding an antiderivative is all you need to evaluate a definite integral.

blocks.title: Antiderivatives and the basic table
blocks.body:
A function $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on an interval if $F' = f$ there. Two antiderivatives of the same function on an interval differ by a constant (their difference has derivative $0$, so it is constant by the mean value theorem). That is why we write
$$\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C.$$
Every entry of the basic table is a derivative from [[diff-rules]] read backwards:
$$\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \ (n \ne -1), \qquad \int \frac{dx}{x} = \ln|x| + C, \qquad \int e^x\,dx = e^x + C,$$
$$\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C, \qquad \int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C, \qquad \int \frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \arctan x + C.$$
The absolute value in $\ln|x|$ matters: for $x < 0$ the derivative of $\ln(-x)$ is $\frac{-1}{-x} = \frac1x$, so the formula works on either side of $0$ (but never across it).

Integrals are linear, $\int (af + bg) = a\int f + b \int g$, but there is no product rule: $\int fg$ is not $\int f \cdot \int g$. Whatever method you use, you can always check the answer by differentiating it.

blocks.title: Substitution rule
blocks.body:
Let $g$ have a continuous derivative on $[a, b]$, and let $f$ be continuous on an interval containing $g([a, b])$. Then
$$\int_a^b f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)\,du.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Since $f$ is continuous, it has an antiderivative $F$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus. By the chain rule, $(F \circ g)'(x) = F'(g(x))\,g'(x) = f(g(x))\,g'(x)$, so $F \circ g$ is an antiderivative of the left-hand integrand. Therefore the left side equals $F(g(b)) - F(g(a))$, and so does the right side.

blocks.title: Using substitution
blocks.body:
In practice you spot an inner function $u = g(x)$ whose derivative also appears as a factor, and write $du = g'(x)\,dx$. For example, with $u = 1 + x^2$, $du = 2x\,dx$:
$$\int_0^2 \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\,dx = \frac12 \int_1^5 \frac{du}{u} = \frac12 \ln 5.$$
Note that the limits changed from $x = 0, 2$ to $u = 1, 5$. If you prefer to keep $x$, find the antiderivative $\frac12 \ln(1 + x^2)$ first and then use the original limits; what you must not do is mix the two.

A substitution does not need the derivative to be visible in advance. For $\int \tan x\,dx = \int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx$, the choice $u = \cos x$ gives $du = -\sin x\,dx$ and
$$\int \tan x\,dx = -\int \frac{du}{u} = -\ln|\cos x| + C.$$

blocks.title: Integration by parts
blocks.body:
If $u$ and $v$ have continuous derivatives on $[a, b]$, then
$$\int_a^b u(x)\,v'(x)\,dx = \Big[u(x)\,v(x)\Big]_a^b - \int_a^b u'(x)\,v(x)\,dx.$$
In indefinite form: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: By the product rule, $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$. All three functions are continuous, so integrating from $a$ to $b$ and using the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\big[uv\big]_a^b = \int_a^b u'v\,dx + \int_a^b uv'\,dx$. Rearrange.

blocks.title: Choosing the parts
blocks.body:
Integration by parts trades $\int u\,v'$ for $\int u'\,v$, so it helps when differentiating $u$ makes it simpler while integrating $v'$ does not make things worse. Polynomials are good choices for $u$ (each differentiation lowers the degree); $e^x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are good choices for $v'$. For instance, with $u = x$ and $v' = \cos x$:
$$\int x \cos x\,dx = x \sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C.$$
Sometimes $v' = 1$ is the right choice. With $u = \ln x$, $v = x$:
$$\int \ln x\,dx = x \ln x - \int x \cdot \frac1x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C.$$
A third pattern is the boomerang. Let $I = \int e^x \sin x\,dx$. Two integrations by parts, each time differentiating the trigonometric factor, give
$$I = e^x \sin x - \int e^x \cos x\,dx = e^x \sin x - e^x \cos x - I,$$
so $2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)$ and $I = \frac12 e^x(\sin x - \cos x) + C$. The unknown integral came back, and we solved for it.

blocks.title: Partial fractions
blocks.body:
A rational function $p(x)/q(x)$ can always be integrated in elementary terms, and the method is algebraic. First, if $\deg p \ge \deg q$, divide to get a polynomial plus a fraction with $\deg p < \deg q$. Next factor $q$. If $q$ is a product of distinct linear factors $(x - r_1)\cdots(x - r_k)$, there are constants with
$$\frac{p(x)}{(x - r_1)\cdots(x - r_k)} = \frac{A_1}{x - r_1} + \cdots + \frac{A_k}{x - r_k},$$
and each piece integrates to $A_i \ln|x - r_i|$. To find $A_i$, multiply both sides by $x - r_i$ and put $x = r_i$: every other term vanishes. (This is the cover-up rule.) For example,
$$\frac{1}{x^2 - 1} = \frac{1}{(x-1)(x+1)} = \frac{1/2}{x - 1} - \frac{1/2}{x+1}, \qquad \int \frac{dx}{x^2 - 1} = \frac12 \ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right| + C.$$
A repeated factor $(x - r)^m$ contributes terms $\frac{A}{x - r} + \cdots + \frac{A'}{(x - r)^m}$, and an irreducible quadratic factor contributes $\frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + bx + c}$, which is handled by completing the square and using $\ln$ and $\arctan$. For instance $$\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 2x + 2} = \int \frac{dx}{(x+1)^2 + 1} = \arctan(x + 1) + C$$.

blocks.title: Trigonometric substitution
blocks.body:
Square roots of quadratics are removed by a substitution that turns the quadratic into a perfect square. For $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ put $x = \sin\theta$ with $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}]$; then $\sqrt{1 - x^2} = \cos\theta$ (positive on this range) and $dx = \cos\theta\,d\theta$. So
$$\int_0^1 \sqrt{1 - x^2}\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^2\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{4},$$
which is the area of a quarter of the unit disc, as it should be. Here the substitution is used from right to left: we replaced $x$ by a function of a new variable. Similarly $x = \tan\theta$ handles $\sqrt{1 + x^2}$ (since $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$).

blocks.title: Repeated integration by parts
blocks.solution:
Take $u = x^2$, $v' = e^x$: $\int x^2 e^x\,dx = x^2 e^x - 2\int x e^x\,dx$. Again with $u = x$: $\int x e^x\,dx = x e^x - e^x$. So an antiderivative is
$$F(x) = x^2 e^x - 2(x e^x - e^x) = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2).$$
Check: $F'(x) = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + e^x(2x - 2) = x^2 e^x$. Hence
$$\int_0^1 x^2 e^x\,dx = F(1) - F(0) = e - 2.$$

blocks.title: A reduction formula
blocks.body: Let $I_n = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^n x\,dx$ for $n \ge 0$. Show that $I_n = \dfrac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$, and compute $I_4$ and $I_5$.
blocks.solution:
Write $\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1} x \cdot \sin x$ and integrate by parts with $u = \sin^{n-1} x$, $v = -\cos x$:
$$I_n = \Big[-\sin^{n-1}x \cos x\Big]_0^{\pi/2} + (n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^{n-2} x \cos^2 x\,dx.$$
The bracket is $0$ at both ends. Replace $\cos^2 x$ by $1 - \sin^2 x$:
$$I_n = (n - 1)(I_{n-2} - I_n), \qquad\text{so}\qquad n I_n = (n-1) I_{n-2}.$$
With $I_0 = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $I_1 = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,dx = 1$:
$$I_4 = \frac34 \cdot \frac12 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{16}, \qquad I_5 = \frac45 \cdot \frac23 \cdot 1 = \frac{8}{15}.$$
In general $I_{2m} = \frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdots (2m-1)}{2 \cdot 4 \cdots (2m)}$, and comparing $I_{2m}$ with its neighbours leads to Wallis's product for $\pi$.

blocks.title: The reflection trick
blocks.solution:
The factor $x$ suggests integration by parts, but with $u = x$ that only trades the problem for $\int \arctan(\cos x)\,dx$, which none of our methods can do. Instead substitute $x = \pi - t$. Since $\sin(\pi - t) = \sin t$ and $\cos^2(\pi - t) = \cos^2 t$, and the limits swap (which cancels the minus sign from $dx = -dt$),
$$I = \int_0^{\pi} \frac{(\pi - t)\sin t}{1 + \cos^2 t}\,dt = \pi\int_0^{\pi} \frac{\sin t}{1 + \cos^2 t}\,dt - I.$$
So $2I = \pi \int_0^{\pi} \frac{\sin t}{1 + \cos^2 t}\,dt$. Now $u = \cos t$, $du = -\sin t\,dt$ turns the remaining integral into
$$\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{du}{1 + u^2} = \arctan 1 - \arctan(-1) = \frac{\pi}{2}.$$
Hence $2I = \frac{\pi^2}{2}$ and $I = \dfrac{\pi^2}{4}$. The general principle, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx$, is one of the most useful tricks for definite integrals in competitions: here we never needed an antiderivative of $\frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}$ at all.

blocks.body:
- Changing variables without changing the limits (or changing them and then substituting back as well).
- Dropping the absolute value in $\int \frac{dx}{x} = \ln|x| + C$.
- Using an antiderivative across a point where the integrand blows up: $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dx}{x^2}$ is not $\big[-\frac1x\big]_{-1}^{1} = -2$ (a positive function cannot have a negative integral); it is an [[improper-integrals|improper integral]] that diverges.
- Assuming $\int f g = \int f \int g$, or $\int \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{\int f}$.
- Expecting every integral to have an elementary answer. The antiderivatives of $e^{-x^2}$, $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ and $\sqrt{1 + x^4}$ cannot be written with the usual functions (a theorem of Liouville). Definite integrals of such functions can still sometimes be computed by other means.
- Using the cover-up rule on a repeated factor as if it gave everything: for $(x - r)^m$ it gives only the coefficient of $\frac{1}{(x - r)^m}$, and the other coefficients must be found another way.

Integrals over unbounded intervals, such as $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx = n!$ (repeated integration by parts), are the subject of [[improper-integrals]] and lead to the [[gamma]] function. Separable [[ode-first|first-order differential equations]] are solved by computing two antiderivatives, often with partial fractions; the logistic equation is a typical case.

Integration by parts is the engine behind the integral form of the remainder in [[taylor|Taylor's theorem]]. Its discrete analogue is Abel summation, and repeated integration by parts gives the Euler–Maclaurin formula; both are in [[partial-summation]]. Integrating a [[power-series]] term by term gives series for $\arctan$ and $\ln(1 + x)$. Integrals over $\mathbb R$ of rational functions, such as $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{1 + x^4}$, are evaluated most easily with [[residues]] in complex analysis.

1. Find $\int x \ln x\,dx$.
2. Find $\int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 4x + 5}$.
3. Show that $\int_0^1 \frac{x^3}{x^2 + 1}\,dx = \frac{1 - \ln 2}{2}$.
4. Let $J_n = \int_0^1 x^n e^x\,dx$. Show that $J_n = e - n J_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$, and deduce that $J_n = a_n e + (-1)^{n+1} n!$ for some integer $a_n$.
